newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Japan says UN should reform, stress development.
newsitem.headline: Japan says UN should reform, stress development.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto called on the United Nations on Tuesday to make "tenacious" reform efforts to fulfil its duty to promote global peace, development and welfare.

"If the United Nations simply engages in repetitious debate and proves incapable of reforming itself to adapt to the changing times, its very credibility could be severely undermined," Hashimoto told the U.N. General Assembly.
He said Japan sought an United Nations better organised to build what the "three pillars" of a better world: peace, economic development and individual well-being.
"We will be unable to achieve a world free of poverty if any one of the three is missing," he said.

Security should be enhanced through efforts to improve rapid response capabilities of U.N. peacekeeping operations and to strengthen the role of the U.N. Preventive Deployment Force and preventive diplomacy mechanisms, he said.

Lauding the signing earlier on Tuesday by U.N. member states of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty as a "historic step toward a world free of nuclear weapons," he called for further measures to curb weapons of mass destruction and land mines.

Reform of the Security Council to expand its membership would enhance the U.N.'s peacekeeping role, Hashimoto said, reiterating the desire of Japan, along with other countries, to join the United States, China, Russia, Britain and France as permanent council members.

"Japan, with the endorsement of many countries, is prepared to discharge its responsibilities as a permanent member of the Security Council in accordance with its basic philosophy of nonresort to the use of force, prohibited by its constitution," he said.
Japan has contributed personnel and logistical support for U.N. peacekeeping operations since 1992, taking part in operations in Cambodia, Angola, Mozambique and the Israeli-controlled Golan Heights.
Economic development efforts by the United Nations should combine trade, investment, economic policy, debt relief, technology transfer and the development of social infrastrusture, Hashimoto said.

Programmes should be carried out "while paying adequate attention to the efforts made by developing countries in the promotion of democratization and the introduction of market-oriented economies," Hashimoto said.

Although he stopped short of specific prescriptions for streamlining the United Nations, Hashimoto suggested that Japan, which will pay 15.65 percent of the 1997 U.N. budget, sought changes to make other countries increase their share of the budget.
"Japan attaches importance not only to the concept of 'capacity to pay' but also to the 'responsibility to pay,'" he said.
Echoing concerns voiced by many Western states, Hashimoto called for "administrative streamlining and rationalising" at the world body."
